content: Workers who are exposed to extreme heat or work in hot environments are at risk of developing heat stress. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can lead to occupational illnesses and injuries, including heat stroke, heat exhaustion, heat cramps, and heat rashes. Additionally, working in hot conditions can increase the likelihood of accidents due to factors such as sweaty palms, fogged safety glasses, and dizziness. Burns may also occur from accidental contact with hot surfaces or steam. Certain groups of workers are particularly vulnerable to heat stress. These include outdoor workers and those employed in hot environments, such as firefighters, bakery workers, farmers, construction workers, miners, boiler room workers, and factory workers. Individuals at greater risk include those aged 65 or older, those who are overweight, individuals with heart disease or high blood pressure, and those taking medications that may be affected by extreme heat. Preventing heat stress is critical for worker safety. Employers should provide comprehensive training to ensure workers understand the risks of heat stress, its impact on health and safety, and effective prevention strategies. The following resources and tools are available to help mitigate heat stress: 1. OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App: This app helps plan outdoor work activities by providing real-time information on how hot it feels throughout the day. It is available in both English and Spanish. 2. NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Heat and Hot Environments: This document offers safety professionals and employers a detailed evaluation of scientific data on heat stress and provides NIOSH recommendations. 3. NIOSH Prevent Heat-Related Illness Poster: A poster with basic reminders for workers exposed to heat and hot environments. 4. NIOSH Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Heat Stress: A free, printable card with essential safety information for workers. 5. NIOSH Infographic: Protect Your Workers from Heat Stress: This infographic provides tips on acclimatization, rest breaks, and fluid intake to protect workers from heat stress. 6. NIOSH-CPWR Infographic: Extreme Heat and Construction Falls: This resource highlights the increased risk of traumatic injuries, such as falls, due to heat exposure. 7. NIOSH Heat Stress: Risk Factors: A guide to understanding the various factors that can influence the risk of heat-related illnesses. 8. NIOSH Heat Stress Podcast: A podcast discussing the symptoms of heat stress and strategies for protection, particularly for indoor and outdoor workers during hot summer months. 9. NIOSH Workplace Solution: Preventing Heat-Related Illness or Death of Outdoor Workers: This document provides employers and safety professionals with case studies and actionable information. 10. OSHA-NIOSH Infosheet: Protecting Workers from Heat Illness: This resource outlines measures employers should take to prevent heat-related illnesses and fatalities. It is also available in ePub format. 11. NIOSH Mining Product: Keeping Cool: Training to Reduce Heat Stress Incidents: A training module designed to help mining workers recognize the signs of heat-related illnesses and administer appropriate first aid. 12. NIOSH Science Blog: Keeping Workers Hydrated and Cool Despite the Heat: This blog emphasizes the importance of hydration and cooling strategies for workers in hot environments. 13. NIOSH Science Blog: Adjusting to Work in the Heat: Why Acclimatization Matters: This blog explains the importance of gradual adaptation to heat and the need for careful planning from a management perspective. 14. NIOSH Science Blog: Extreme Heat – Are You Prepared for Summer Work?: A reminder of the importance of recognizing and preventing the harmful effects of excessive heat as summer approaches. 15. MMWR: Heat Illness and Death Among Workers – United States, 2012-2013: A report summarizing findings from OSHA federal enforcement cases related to heat stress. 16. MMWR: Heat-Related Deaths Among Crop Workers, 1992-2006: A report detailing heat-related fatalities among crop production workers in the United States. 17. CDC: Extreme Heat: Additional information on heat-related illnesses and prevention strategies. 18. National Integrated Heat Health Information System (NIHHIS): A system designed to enhance understanding of extreme heat and improve communication, capacity, and societal awareness of the issue.
